d_intro_1: There! A page of the Atlas blew in here. Its ink has gone pale.
d_intro_2: Pale ink needs light. But this room is kept dark.
d_intro_3: One thin beam comes in by the shutter. Let us turn the mirrors and send it to the page!
d_scholar_1: Welcome, small travellers. I am testing how light moves.
d_scholar_2: It runs straight until something turns it or stops it. Try my mirrors and see.
c_thanks: Thank you. We will try the mirrors.
d_scholar_dark_1: In a dark room, one thin beam is easy to follow. You can stop it with your hand, or measure it with a ruler.
d_scholar_dark_2: So the dark is not for hiding. It is for seeing better!
d_scholar_see_1: The museum's record says older books had sight leap out of the eye. He held the opposite: light comes from the thing to the eye.
d_scholar_see_2: So when I look at you, your light is visiting me.
d_scholar_see_2_f: So when I look at you, your light is visiting me.
d_scholar_bye: Test it yourselves. That is the best way to know.
d_scholar_after: A straight beam, turned five times. You did not take my word for it: you tried.

d_cat_3: She has found the warmest spot in the room.

note_1: Ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra around the year 965 and later lived in Cairo. His best-known book is on optics: light and sight.
note_2: The museum's record says he let light into a dark room through a small hole, to test that it travels in straight lines and that a solid body cuts it.
note_3: The same record says he held that light goes from the thing to the eye.
note_uncertain: Not from the records: this workshop, its cat and the mirrors on stands are invented for the game. The founder's pictures of this story show a glass prism; no museum record read for the scene says he used one, so the game does not show one.

ck_note_2: From the museum's record: al-Jazari described this clock in his book of machines, which one reference work dates to 1205. Every half hour figures move, a ball passes from the falcon to the dragon to a vessel with a gong, and the balls gathered tell the time.
ck_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game stands the parts in one row and has each set the next going. The record describes levers, chains and strings inside the elephant, and what was read for this game does not say how the falcon is made to let its ball go.
ck_note_4: The record does not call him the inventor of clocks or of robots. It says he improved display clocks and moving figures within an older tradition.

pro_1: In a quiet museum sleeps a great book, the Atlas of Stories. Every page holds the story of a person, a place or an invention.
pro_2: One night a storm blew the window open. Fifty pages flew out of the Atlas and scattered across ten worlds.
pro_3: Hudhud saw it all. Hudhud is a curious hoopoe with an orange crest who lives among the museum's shelves.
pro_4: In the morning Hudhud found you beside the empty Atlas. "I know the way," he said, "and you know how to ask. Let us bring the pages home together!"
pro_5: A page comes home when you understand its story: by a question, by a clever idea, or by a kindness. The Atlas and the storm are invented. The people and places behind the pages are real, or are stories marked as stories, and the museum keeps what it knows of them.

cf_count_1: The museum's record says al-Kindi wrote the earliest treatise on breaking ciphers that survives. In it he counts the letters of a long sample of the language, ranks them from most to fewest, and compares that with the symbols of the secret message.
cf_short_1: He warns that a short message can mislead. And he tests a guess by looking at which letters stand side by side and at the usual openings of messages.

ak_intro_1: The page of the Atlas is folded inside a box, and the box opens only for the right number!
ak_intro_2: Call the unknown a thing, then bring the problem to its simplest form.
ak_words_1: The museum's record says al-Khwarizmi wrote everything in words, not symbols: the unknown is a thing or a root, and the known amount is a number or dirhams.
ak_ops_1: His book is named after two operations: al-jabr, restoring, which removes what is taken away on one side by adding its like to both sides; and al-muqabala, balancing, which cancels like terms on both sides.
ak_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The locked box, the two trays, the three problems, the child who carries the box and every spoken line are invented for play.
ak_note_2: From the museum's record: al-Khwarizmi's book on al-jabr and al-muqabala brings every problem to one of six types, each with a rule and a proof by a figure. He wrote it for what people need in inheritances, trade and the measuring of land.
ak_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game's problems are of the simplest type, things equal to a number. The step of sharing among the things is the game's own. Nothing read for this game says he used trays or a pair of scales.
ak_note_4: The record says that solving equations is older than him, in Babylon, among the Greeks and in India, and that Ibn Khaldun names him as the first to write in this art.

jz_intro_1: The page of the Atlas is hidden among the animal cards, and the cards have lost their groups!
jz_intro_2: Do not judge by feathers or by wings alone. See what people call each one.
jz_divide_1: The museum's record says al-Jahiz divided animals in his book by how they move: those that walk, fly, swim or creep. He says that in this he follows the names known among the people of his language.
jz_birds_1: He notes that not everything that flies on two wings is a bird: locusts, bees and flies fly but are not called birds; the bat is counted among the birds though it has no feathers; and the ostrich has feathers but is not, for him, a bird.
jz_hoopoe_1: The record lists the hoopoe among the creatures in the third part of his book.
jz_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The cards, the trays, the girl who carries the cards and every spoken line are invented for play.
jz_note_2: From the museum's record: al-Jahiz divides animals into those that walk, fly, swim or creep, and among birds of prey he tells those armed with talons, like the eagle, from those armed with beaks, like vultures and crows. All eight creatures in the game are named in this passage of his book.
jz_note_3: This is al-Jahiz's division, more than a thousand years old, and it follows the names used by the people of his language. Science today sorts animals in another way: it counts the bat among the mammals and the ostrich among the birds.
jz_note_4: Made simpler for play: the game takes one passage of the Book of Animals. The record says the book is wider than its title, with language, customs and much other learning in it.

pp_intro_1: The page of the Atlas was soaked in the storm and torn. We need a new sheet!
pp_intro_2: Paper is made step by step, and each step has its place. But the cards of the steps are mixed up.
pp_story_1: The museum's record says an old report tells that Chinese craftsmen captured in a battle near the Talas river in 751 taught the people of Samarkand to make paper from worn-out rags. The record calls this a report handed down, not a proved beginning.
pp_how_1: The record gives the way it was made: rags of linen or hemp are cut small, cleaned and bleached, then pounded in water to a pulp and dressed with wheat starch, then lifted on a mould and shaken until the fibres hold together. The sheet is laid flat and dried on a wall, then rubbed and polished smooth.
pp_child_1: I hung the cards of the steps on a line to dry, and the wind blew them down. Now I cannot tell where each one goes!
pp_child_kind: It is all right. We will put them in order together.
pp_child_blunt: You should have pegged them to the line.
pp_child_kind_r: Thank you! Next time I will peg every card.
pp_child_blunt_r: I know. Next time I will peg every card.
pp_feather_1: A feather, caught in the mould! It is one of mine.
pp_feather_again: Nothing else is caught in the mould.
pp_done_1: The sheet is smooth, and the page of the Atlas is whole again!
pp_goal_curiosity_how: Ask both questions: about the old report and about how paper was made.
pp_goal_ingenuity_how: Make a sheet in {n} moves or fewer.
pp_goal_kindness_how: Answer the child who helps kindly.
pp_goal_feather_how: Find the feather in the mould.
pp_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The workshop, the papermaker, the child who helps, the cards of the steps, and every spoken line, are invented for play.
pp_note_2: From the museum's record: the Chinese invented paper. The part of the Islamic world was to receive the craft, adapt it and spread it. From Samarkand it moved to Baghdad, and on to Egypt, Damascus, the Maghrib, Jativa in Spain and other lands.
pp_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game makes each step one card in a row. For the pounding the record names mortars, stampers and paper-mills; the game shows one mallet.

ib_intro_1: The page of the Atlas has flown along a traveller's road. Let us follow his road, stop by stop!
ib_intro_2: A road is remembered by its order: where you set out, and then where next.
ib_left_1: The museum's record says Ibn Battuta left Tangier on Thursday the second of Rajab in the year 725 of the Hijra for the pilgrimage, alone, aged twenty-two.
ib_written_1: It says he did not write his journey down himself: Sultan Abu Inan ordered it written, Ibn Battuta dictated it, and Ibn Juzayy edited it.
ib_stage_story: He left Tangier and crossed North Africa, Egypt, Upper Egypt and Syria, then left Damascus for Mecca.
ib_stage_explorer: He went down the Red Sea to Yemen and Aden, then to Zayla, Mogadishu and the trading ports of East Africa, and came back by Oman and the Persian Gulf.
ib_stage_challenge: He left Mecca and went through Iraq, Khuzistan, Fars and the Jibal, then to Tabriz, Baghdad, Samarra and Mosul, and then returned to Baghdad.
ib_child_1: My camel has lost its bell, and I cannot hear where the caravan has gone. I am afraid of being left behind!
ib_child_kind: Do not be afraid. We will follow the thread together.
ib_child_blunt: You should have kept closer to the caravan.
ib_child_kind_r: Thank you! I will hold the camel's rope tightly.
ib_child_blunt_r: I know. Next time I will keep closer.
ib_feather_1: A feather, caught in the saddlebag! It is one of mine.
ib_feather_again: Nothing else is caught in the saddlebag.
ib_done_1: The thread is complete. The page of the Atlas can land and rest.
ib_goal_curiosity_how: Ask both questions: about when he set out and about who wrote his journey down.
ib_goal_ingenuity_how: Slips allowed: {n}. Thread the stage without going over that number.
ib_goal_ingenuity_story: Thread the stage to its end.
ib_goal_kindness_how: Answer the child with the camel kindly.
ib_goal_feather_how: Find the feather in the saddlebag.
ib_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The thread, the beads, the child with the camel and every spoken line are invented for play. The picture is not a map: the beads sit on a ring, with no direction and no distance meant.
ib_note_2: From the museum's record: the record sets Ibn Battuta's journeys out in eight stages, after an article in an encyclopaedia. The game follows three of them.
ib_note_3: The record says scholars do not take everything in the account as it stands: Ibn Battuta told of losing some of his travel notes and writing them again from memory, and the article holds that the editor of the account rearranged several of its routes. The order here is the order of the account as that article sets it out.
ib_rec_question: the question of believing his reports
